content: The World Health Organization (WHO) conducted extensive preparatory work, including policy reviews, literature reviews, and mathematical modeling, to support the development of its guidelines. WHO also compiled examples of good practices, which are accessible in Web Annex K. Policy Reviews WHO reviewed national HIV testing services (HTS) policies from 146 countries, focusing primarily on lowand middle-income countries, to evaluate the adoption of WHO recommendations and guidance. A standardized protocol, initially developed for the 2015 Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, was adapted for this review. Two reviewers were involved in the process, and policies were translated as necessary. The uptake of policies was further assessed using data from the 2019 Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) survey conducted by WHO, UNAIDS, and UNICEF. Indicators related to HTS policy uptake were validated between April and July 2019 based on country reports. The policy repository and GAM survey addressed several key topics: 1. Adoption and implementation of WHO Consolidated Guidelines and guidance on HIV self-testing (HIVST) and assisted partner notification. 2. Uptake of national policies and operational guidance on HIVST. 3. Retesting policies, including maternal retesting during pregnancy and postpartum, as well as among key populations. 4. Age of consent for HIV testing. 5. Adoption of WHO HIV testing strategies and algorithms. 6. Integration of HTS into family planning clinics. 7. Use of risk screening tools to optimize HTS. Mathematical Modeling Mathematical modeling was employed to refine existing WHO recommendations and address operational questions regarding their implementation. Specific modeling efforts included: Assessing the accuracy and performance of HIV testing strategies in response to changes in the global HIV epidemic. This modeling provided implementation considerations for WHO guidance recommending three consecutive reactive tests to confirm an HIV-positive diagnosis in settings with an HIV positivity rate below 5%. Determining the optimal and most cost-effective time points for maternal retesting among women with negative or unknown HIV status in highand low-HIV burden settings. This modeling supported WHO guidance recommending maternal retesting during late pregnancy and the postpartum period in high-burden settings. Evaluating the use of dual HIV/syphilis tests in antenatal care for pregnant and postpartum women in highand low-burden settings. This modeling informed WHO recommendations on dual testing among pregnant women. Development and Dissemination of Guidelines Following consultations with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and external reviewers, WHO revised the draft guidelines and circulated them for feedback. All responses were considered and addressed in the final draft. The guidelines were made available through the WHO website, the HTS Info app, and print publications. Links to all web annexes were included for easy reference. To facilitate understanding, policy briefs and slide sets summarizing the recommendations were developed. WHO headquarters collaborated with regional and country offices, as well as implementing partners, to disseminate the guidelines through regional and sub-regional meetings. Member States were supported in adapting the guidelines to their national contexts. WHO also committed to monitoring the uptake and implementation of the guidelines through bi-annual GAM surveys, policy reviews, and dialogues with countries and partners. The HTS Info app was used to monitor guideline usage and provide complementary content. Future Updates WHO plans to review and potentially update the guidance in 2024–2025. In the interim, if significant new evidence emerges, technical and programmatic updates may be issued. Implementation tools and materials will be developed in collaboration with Member States and regional offices to support further implementation efforts. Key Points on Demand Creation Concise, informative, and motivational communication prior to HIV testing is effective in creating demand for HTS among individuals unaware of their HIV status and those at high ongoing risk, without increasing stigma or discrimination. An enabling environment that removes barriers such as stigma, discrimination, criminalization, and age of consent issues is crucial for increasing access to HTS, particularly for high-risk and key populations. Demand creation efforts should prioritize individuals at high risk who have never tested or have not tested recently, as well as HIV-positive individuals aware of their status but not in care. Evidence-based approaches to demand creation include peer-led and digital platforms, advertising specific HTS attributes, motivational messages, and risk-reduction messaging. WHO does not recommend pre-test counseling but instead advocates for concise pre-test information that answers questions and allows individuals to refuse testing if desired. Demand creation efforts should include messages explaining the benefits of early antiretroviral therapy (ART) and the fact that individuals with undetectable viral loads cannot transmit HIV to their partners. Integrating brief HIV-specific information and counseling messages into broader health visits and prevention packages may be beneficial, particularly in high-burden settings. Considerations for Incentives While incentives can increase HTS uptake, their use should be carefully evaluated for potential risks, including resource sustainability, equity concerns, and the potential to deprioritize systematic implementation of strategies that improve service delivery and reduce barriers.
